column4: The section links 88:22’s مُصَيْطِر to the root س ط ر and says the true record is God’s. In the Qamar passage about earlier peoples, مُسْتَطَر states that every small and great thing is written, making that transfer of record-keeping explicit.

The section says the Prophet is no مُصَيْطِر and that rejecting people are not overseers either. This other Quranic use asks whether the deniers possess their Lord’s خزائن or are themselves مُصَيْطِرُون, locating such authority beyond them.

The section connects the overseer’s supposed writing of deeds to God’s record. This preceding Qamar verse says everything they did is in the writings; 54:53 specifies that every small and great thing is inscribed.

The section says the deeds are recorded and will be accounted for. At the Judgment, sinners see a register that leaves out neither small nor great, and find what they did present; this makes the record’s completeness concrete.
The section transfers oversight from the Prophet to God. This verse says no matter, Quran recitation, or human act is hidden from God, down to the smallest and largest thing, all in a clear record.

The section says the hand that writes deeds is not the Prophet’s. God says “We write” what people send ahead and their traces, and has counted everything in a clear register, specifying the divine record and its reach.

The section distinguishes the Prophet from a recorder who watches people’s states and writes their deeds. When deniers suppose their secret speech is unheard, the verse answers that God’s messengers with them are writing it down.

The section rejects the Prophet’s role as keeper over people. This Judgment passage instead introduces keepers assigned over them; 82:11 identifies them as writers and 82:12 says they know what people do.
The section says the true record of deeds belongs to God. Here the keepers introduced in 82:10 are explicitly كِرَامًا كَاتِبِينَ, “honorable writers”; 82:12 specifies what their record concerns.
The section describes deeds being written for later account. This verse says the appointed writers know what people do, completing 82:10–11’s scene of record-keepers.
The section describes a watcher set over people who attends their state and writes their action. Here two receivers sit on the right and left; 50:18 says each spoken word has a ready observer.
The section’s lexical gloss calls a watcher a رَقِيب who attends to what is entrusted to him. This verse says each word has رَقِيبٌ عَتِيدٌ, completing 50:17’s scene of two receivers.

The section says the Prophet is not the one who keeps the record and that God will account for deeds. At the Judgment, each community’s book speaks truth, and God says it has been copying what they did.

The section’s distinction between a reminder and a watcher ends in divine accounting. Here each person is brought a book on the Resurrection Day, spread open; 17:14 tells them to read it and says the self is enough as its accountant.
The section assigns حساب to God after people return. This continuation tells each person to read their book and says the self is enough as حَسِيبًا; 17:13 supplies the opened record.

The section links the lexical sense of سطر to lining things up and names cushions as مُصَفَّفَة in the garden. Here all are presented before their Lord in rows, making ordered lines part of the Judgment scene that leads into 18:49’s complete register.

The section says every person returns for حساب. God sets just balances for Judgment, wrongs no soul at all, and brings even a mustard seed’s weight; the verse ends by calling God an adequate accountant.

The section says the Prophet is not the keeper placed over people. This verse says God is dominant over His servants and sends keepers over them until death; 6:62 continues with their return and accounting before God.

The section says “to Us is their return” and “their account is upon Us.” This verse likewise says they are returned to God, their true Mawla, who owns judgment and is the swiftest of accountants; 6:61 describes the keepers until death.
The section assigns both return and account to God. This verse says people will return to Him and He will tell them what they did, while knowing everything.
The section says each person will return to God for account. This verse says no soul bears another’s burden, then names the return to the Lord, who will tell them what they disputed.
The section gives حساب to God. This Judgment verse says every soul is paid in full for what it did, while God knows what they do, showing the personal outcome of that account.
The section says the final account is God’s. This verse says God has a book that speaks truth and that people will not be wronged, so the divine record and just reckoning stand together.
The section says God accounts for deeds. This verse says whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it; 99:8 gives the corresponding result for evil.
The section says God accounts for deeds. This verse says whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it, completing 99:7’s matching statement about good.

The section says a person who turns away and disbelieves faces God’s account. This verse says every soul is held by what it earned, expressing personal accountability without making the Prophet its keeper.

The section transfers judgment from the Prophet to God and says people return for account. This verse draws the boundary sharply: God is not questioned about what He does, while they will be questioned.

The section explains سطر as a line of writing and connects it to the record of deeds. This Quranic oath invokes the pen and what it writes, giving the root’s writing sense a direct Quranic occurrence.
The section’s س ط ر discussion moves from rows to writing. Here the oath names a كِتَابٍ مَسْطُورٍ, a written book; it supplies the same root in the writing sense.
The section links the line sense of سطر with the garden cushions described as مُصَفَّفَة. This opening oath names those who line up in صفًّا, a distinct Quranic scene of ordered ranks.

The section names the cushions’ صفّ arrangement and connects it to the lexical sense of lining things up. Here the speaker says, “we are the ones in ranks,” repeating 37:1’s ranked scene in the same surah.

The section’s صفّ image is a row of garden cushions, while this verse uses صفًّا for believers fighting in God’s path, like a solid structure. It makes the same ordered line serve a different, active purpose.
The section connects the cushion word مُصَفَّفَة with the meaning of things set in rows. Here the Spirit and angels stand صفًّا on the day they rise, placing the same order in a Judgment scene.
The section links lined cushions with the sense of صفّ and places their arrangement beside God’s later accounting. Here the angels stand صفًّا صفًّا; 89:23 continues with Hell brought near.
The section calls the cushions مُصَفَّفَة and explains the underlying sense as lining things up. In Moses’s contest, the magicians are told to come صفًّا, another concrete use of the row image.

The section denies that the Prophet is the overseer and gives punishment to God. After recalling destroyed peoples, this verse says the Lord is لَبِالْمِرْصَادِ, placing the watchful station with God.
The section says the Prophet’s task is reminder and “their account is upon Us.” This verse gives the same division in one sentence: the Prophet’s is only the delivery, and the account is upon God.

The section says “remind” and denies that the Prophet is set over people as a controller. This verse says he is not a جَبَّار over them and commands him to remind by the Quran whoever fears God’s warning.
The section says the Prophet is not a keeper over people. This verse says he was not sent as their حَفِيظ and that only clear delivery is upon him.
The section says the Prophet is neither their overseer nor their guardian. This verse says God did not make him حَفِيظ over them and that he is not their وكيل.
The section gives punishment to God rather than to the Prophet. This verse says God may show mercy or punish, and that the Prophet was not sent as their وكيل.
The section restricts the Prophet’s role to reminder, not control. This verse asks whether he would compel people until they became believers, making coercion the very boundary the section draws.

The section says the Prophet is not a keeper over people. This verse says whoever sees benefits himself and whoever is blind bears it against himself, then states that the Prophet is not their حَفِيظ.
The section says the Prophet is not a monitor over people. This verse says whoever turns away has his own path, for the Prophet was not sent as their حَفِيظ.
The section distinguishes reminder from control and later account. This verse says guidance benefits the person and misguidance falls on them, then denies that the Prophet is their وكيل.

The section says the Prophet is not responsible for keeping people and that their account belongs to God. This verse says the one guided benefits himself, the one astray bears it, and the Prophet is not their وكيل.
The section denies that the Prophet is people’s keeper. This verse explicitly assigns حفيظ status over them to God and says the Prophet is not their وكيل.
The section reduces the Prophet’s task to reminding, not controlling people. This verse calls him only a warner and says God is وكيل over all things.

The section says the Prophet is not the people’s guardian and should remind those who respond. This verse says no bearer carries another’s burden, the Prophet is not their وكيل, and he warns those who fear their Lord.
The section calls the Prophet مُذَكِّر, a reminder. This verse states that he is only a نَذِير, a warner, specifying a related but distinct part of his limited commission.
The section denies that the Prophet is placed over people as their overseer. After describing someone who takes desire as a god, this verse asks whether the Prophet would be that person’s وكيل.

The section distinguishes the Prophet’s reminder from people’s response. This verse says if they turn away, the Messenger bears only his charge and they bear theirs; if they obey, they are guided, and only clear delivery is upon him.
The section says people who turn away remain outside the Prophet’s control. This verse says that if they turn away, only clear delivery is upon the Messenger.
The section gives the Prophet reminder rather than oversight. This verse says that if people turn away, the Messenger’s only duty is clear delivery.
The section makes the Prophet a reminder, not an overseer. This verse says only delivery is upon the Messenger and that God knows what people reveal and conceal.
The section draws a limit around the Prophet’s task. This verse tells those addressed that if they turn away, the Messenger’s only duty is clear delivery.
The section says the Prophet’s work is reminder rather than control. This verse says if they turn away, only delivery is upon him, while God sees His servants.

The section denies that the Prophet’s responsibility is to control belief. In this verse, after people excuse their disbelief by appeal to God’s will, the reply asks whether messengers have any duty beyond clear delivery.
The section says refusal does not turn the Prophet into an overseer. Here, after the address turns to those who deny, it says the Messenger’s only duty is clear delivery.
The section limits the Prophet’s responsibility for people’s response to reminder. This verse says their guidance is not upon him; God guides whom He wills.
The section denies that the Prophet can control people’s response. This verse says he does not guide whom he loves; God guides whom He wills.
The section rejects coercion in the Prophet’s role. This verse states there is no compulsion in religion and distinguishes right guidance from error.
The section says the Prophet’s task is reminder, not command over outcomes. This verse says he follows only what is revealed and is only a clear warner.
The section says the Prophet reminds those who fear. This verse states directly that he is only a warner for the one who fears the Hour.
The section calls the Prophet’s task reminder and cites the one who fears. This verse says the Quran was sent as a تَذْكِرَة for whoever fears, tying the reminder to that audience.

The section begins with the command to remind and rejects a controlling role. This verse says “so remind” and denies that the Prophet is a soothsayer or madman, framing reminder as his actual commission.

The section cites the previous surah’s sequence: remind, then people respond differently. This verse commands reminder when it benefits; 87:10 identifies the one who will remember, and 87:11 the one who turns away.

The section cites the response to reminder: the one who fears remembers, while the denier turns away. This verse says the reminder will be taken by the one who fears; 87:9 gives the command and 87:11 the contrary response.
The section says the one who turns away and disbelieves receives God’s punishment. This verse says the most wretched will avoid the reminder; 87:12 names the great Fire that follows.

The section cites the sequence in which one avoids the reminder and God punishes. This verse names the great Fire entered by the most wretched, completing 87:11’s refusal and leading toward the section’s punishment.
The section defines tezkire as a means of remembering and makes reminder the Prophet’s task. This verse commands reminder because the reminder benefits believers.
The section names tezkire as a means of bringing something to mind. This verse calls the Quran a تَذْكِرَة; 80:12 says whoever wishes may remember it.
The section says reminder leaves room for a person’s response. Here whoever wishes may remember the تذكرة named in 80:11.
The section names a reminder as the instrument that brings something back to mind. This verse says the Quran is a تَذْكِرَة; 74:55 gives the hearer’s choice to remember.
The section says the Prophet reminds but does not control the response. This verse says whoever wills may remember the تذكرة named in 74:54; 74:56 bounds that will by God’s will.
The section gives the Prophet a limited role and God final authority over punishment and account. This verse says people do not remember unless God wills, completing 74:54–55’s reminder and choice.
The section defines تذكرة as a thing that brings remembrance and says the Prophet’s role is reminder. This verse calls the revelation a تَذْكِرَة and lets whoever wills take a path to their Lord.

The section’s reminder leaves the hearer responsible for a response. This verse says the revelation is a تَذْكِرَة and whoever wills may take a path to their Lord; 76:30 adds that human willing remains under God’s will.
The section denies the Prophet control over people and assigns final judgment to God. This verse says people do not will unless God wills, completing 76:29’s invitation to choose a path.
The section calls the Prophet a reminder and defines tezkire as what brings remembrance. This verse says the Quran is a ذكر for the worlds; 81:28 names its audience as those who choose uprightness.
The section allows for people to respond differently to reminder. This verse addresses those among the hearers who will to be upright; 81:29 says even their will is within God’s will.
The section distinguishes the Prophet’s limited role from God’s authority over outcomes. This verse says people do not will unless God wills, completing 81:27–28’s reminder and response.

The section says remembrance is repeated and that the Prophet brings the Quran to mind. After Noah’s people in the Qamar narrative, this refrain says the Quran is made easy for remembrance and asks who will remember.

The section connects reminder with people’s response and with accounts of earlier peoples. After the account of ʿAd, the same refrain says the Quran is easy for remembrance and asks who will remember.
The section connects reminder with the response of those who hear it. After Thamud’s rejection, this repeated Qamar refrain asks who will remember the Quran made easy for remembrance.

The section describes a reminder that may be accepted or refused and ends with punishment. After the account of Lot’s people, this refrain again asks who will remember the Quran made easy for remembrance.
The section says the reminder is repeated and that some turn away. This verse says Quranic examples were varied so people might remember, yet they only become more averse.
The section defines zikra as repeated remembrance. This verse says examples are given throughout the Quran so that people may remember.

The section calls the Prophet a reminder and defines tezkire as something that brings remembrance. After the accusation that the Prophet is a madman, this verse says the Quran is a reminder for the worlds.
The section says the Prophet’s function is reminder. This verse identifies the Quran as a reminder for the worlds, in the passage that refutes claims about the revelation.
The section describes the Quranic message as what brings remembrance. This verse calls the revelation a reminder for the worlds after recalling the prophets who were guided.

The section connects turning away and disbelief with God’s punishment. This verse warns of a blazing Fire; 92:15 says only the most wretched will enter it, and 92:16 identifies him as the denier who turns away.
The section links a person’s turning away to the punishment God gives. This verse says only the most wretched enters the blazing Fire named in 92:14; 92:16 specifies his denial and turning away.

The section’s exception is the one who turns away and disbelieves, followed by God’s punishment. This verse describes the same figure as one who كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى, after the warning of the Fire in 92:14–15.

The section’s exception turns away and disbelieves; the previous surah’s sequence likewise says one avoids the reminder. This verse says to leave the one who turns away from God’s remembrance and seeks only this nearer life; 53:30 says God knows who strays and who is guided.

The section says the turn-away is followed by God’s punishment and that return is to Him. This continuation says God knows who has strayed and who is guided, completing 53:29’s person turning away from remembrance.
The section says the one who turns away and disbelieves will be punished by God. This verse says that if they turn away, God will punish them with painful punishment.
The section says people return to God for account. This Judgment passage begins the two outcomes with the person given his book in his right hand; 84:8 says he will have an easy account.
The section assigns حساب to God. This verse says the person who receives his book in his right hand will be given an easy account, completing 84:7; 84:9 describes his return happy.
The section says people return to God and are accounted for. This verse shows the positive outcome as the person returns to his people joyfully after the easy account of 84:8.
The section says the one who turns away will face punishment after account. This verse presents the other Judgment outcome: the person receives his book behind his back; 84:11 gives his response.
The section says God punishes the one who turned away. Here the person whose book is given behind his back calls for destruction, after the scene in 84:10 and before the Fire in 84:12.
The section says God gives the greatest punishment after people return to Him. This verse names the outcome for the person whose book is behind his back: he enters a blazing Fire.
The section ends by saying people return to God for account. This verse asks whether people thought they were created aimlessly and would not be returned; 23:116 identifies God as the true King.
The section assigns return and account to God. This continuation names God the true King, the only deity, and Lord of the noble Throne, completing the challenge to deny return in 23:115.
The section says everyone returns to God for account. This verse describes the Day every soul pleads for itself and is paid in full for what it did, without being wronged.

The section’s dictionary note glosses إله as Allah because He is the one worshipped. In this verse Allah identifies Himself as the only deity and commands Moses to worship Him, connecting the name to the gloss.

The section notes that تَوَلَّى can have the secondary sense of taking up a task or office. This verse names أُولِي الْأَمْر, those entrusted with authority, and directs disputes back to God and the Messenger, making delegated authority distinct from the Prophet’s role as everyone’s overseer.

The section says the Prophet is not the one appointed to account for people. This verse tells him not to dismiss those who call on their Lord, saying their account is not upon him and his account is not upon them; it makes the boundary of حساب explicit.
The section denies that the Prophet is an overseer over those who refuse the reminder. After his people reject the truth, this verse has him say that he is not their وكيل.

The section separates the Prophet’s reminder from God’s punishment and final account. This verse says guidance benefits the person, no bearer carries another’s burden, and God does not punish until sending a messenger.

The section says people may turn away and disbelieve, after which God punishes. This verse commands the Prophet to state that whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve, then names the Fire prepared for wrongdoers.

The section describes a person turning away from reminder and later being accounted for. This verse speaks of one reminded of his Lord’s signs who turns away from them and forgets what his hands sent ahead, joining refusal to neglected deeds.

The section names turning away and disbelief as the response that leads to God’s punishment. This verse explicitly speaks of turning away from God’s remembrance and gives a consequence in this life and the Resurrection.

The section says the one who turns away and disbelieves is punished by God. This verse asks who is more unjust than the person reminded of his Lord’s signs who then turns away, and says God will take retribution on the criminals.

The section says the exception to reminder is one who turns away, followed by God’s judgment. This verse describes one who turns aside from the remembrance of the Merciful, to whom God assigns a companion that leads him away.
The section denies the Prophet control over people and assigns punishment to God. This verse tells him he has no say in the affair, whether God turns to people in mercy or punishes them.

The section makes reminding the Prophet’s task and says people bear their own response. This verse commands him to recite the Quran and says whoever is guided benefits himself, while the Prophet is only among the warners.

The section says if people turn away, the Prophet’s duty remains reminder and the outcome belongs to God. Hud says that if they turn away he has delivered what he was sent with, and that his Lord is keeper over everything.
The section says the Prophet is not the people’s وكيل and that God owns judgment. This verse says God created everything and is وكيل over everything, locating that encompassing role with God.

The section notes a secondary sense of و ل ي as taking up a task or office. This verse describes believing men and women as one another’s awliya and assigns them shared work: enjoining right, forbidding wrong, prayer, and almsgiving.

The section glosses تَوَلَّى as turning one’s back. This verse describes turning one’s back in battle and warns of returning with God’s anger, a concrete physical use of that turning-away image in a different setting.
The section says people return to God for account. This verse warns of a day when they will be returned to God and every soul paid in full for what it earned, without being wronged.
The section assigns the final accounting to God. This verse says God will question both the communities to whom messengers were sent and the messengers themselves, placing the accounting with Him.

The section says God will account for people after their return. This verse states under an oath by the Lord that He will question them all; 15:93 specifies that the question is about what they used to do.
The section says people are returned for account before God. This verse identifies the subject of His questioning in 15:92: what they used to do.
The section says God will account for those who turn away. This verse commands that they be stopped because they are to be questioned, making the Judgment’s interrogation explicit.
The section says the final account and punishment are God’s. This verse says the day every soul is repaid for what it earned, with no injustice.

The section says people return to God for their account. This Judgment scene shows every community kneeling and being called to its book, with each repaid for what it did; 45:29 describes the book’s truth and its writing.

The section says the return and accounting belong to God. This Judgment verse places the book, brings prophets and witnesses, and says judgment between people is done in truth; 39:70 says each soul is paid for its deeds.

The section describes people returning for account and rejects the Prophet as their overseer. This verse says each soul arrives with a driver and a witness; 50:22 describes the unveiling of what had been overlooked.
The section says people will return for God’s account. This verse says the person had been heedless of this day, then has the covering removed; 50:21 introduces each soul with a driver and witness.
The section says people’s deeds will be accounted for by God. This verse says hearing, sight, and the heart will each be questioned, extending accountability to what a person perceives and intends.
The section says the Prophet is not the final judge and that account belongs to God. This verse says that whatever people differ over, its judgment belongs to Allah.

The section says the Prophet is not the overseer who imposes the outcome. This verse tells him to leave the deniers until they meet the day promised to them, assigning the encounter to God’s coming judgment.

The section says the Prophet’s task is reminder, while those who reject it face their promised outcome. This verse tells the Prophet to leave the deniers in their talk and play until they meet the promised day.

The section says those who turn away will meet God’s punishment. This verse tells the Prophet to leave the deniers until they meet their promised day; 70:43 describes their emergence from graves to the caller.

The section says people return for account and punishment. This verse depicts them emerging quickly from their graves toward the caller on that promised day; 70:42 names the meeting awaiting the deniers.

The section says God punishes the one who turns away and disbelieves. In this Judgment passage, Hell is brought forward; 89:24 shows the person remembering too late and wishing he had sent something ahead.
The section says a person’s deeds are accounted for after return. This verse shows the person remembering and regretting what he did when Hell is brought forward in 89:23.
The section says Allah gives the greatest punishment to the one who turns away. This verse says no one punishes as He punishes.
The section gives punishment to Allah rather than the Prophet. This verse says no one binds as He binds, emphasizing that final restraint belongs to God.

The section places Paradise’s furnishings beside the later return to God. This verse addresses the tranquil soul before the command to return in 89:28, introducing the rewarded side of the Judgment scene.
The section says “to Us is their return.” This verse commands the pleased and accepted soul to return to its Lord, followed by entry among God’s servants in 89:29 and into His Garden in 89:30.

The section joins return to God with the Garden scene whose cushions are arranged. This verse invites the returned soul to enter among God’s servants; 89:30 completes the invitation with entry into His Garden.
The section begins with ordered furnishings in the Garden and ends with people returning for account. This verse completes the positive Judgment outcome by inviting the soul into God’s Garden.
The section cites the previous surah’s sequence from reminder to avoidance and the great Fire. This verse says the one in that Fire neither dies nor lives, completing the consequence named in 87:12.
The section cites the sequence in which the fearful remember and the most wretched avoid the reminder. This next verse names the contrasting outcome: success belongs to the one who purifies himself.
The section links reminder with the response of the one who fears. This verse says the successful person remembers his Lord’s name and prays, completing 87:14’s description of success.
The section cites reminder, refusal, and the great Fire. This verse gives a motive for refusal: people prefer the nearer life; 87:17 contrasts the hereafter as better and more enduring.
The section says the one who rejects reminder faces the great Fire. This verse contrasts that nearer-life preference with the hereafter, which is better and more enduring, completing 87:16.
